record.paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can a reconfigurable intelligent surface element be completely deactivated so that its reflection is nulled with respect to all angles, and what physically realizable RIS design or control model would make that all-angle nulling possible for channel-training methods that rely on turning elements off?

evidence.quote: Nulling the reflection of an RIS element with respect to all angles has not been adequately addressed in the literature and remains an open issue. See Section IX for further details.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of $N$ subwavelength reflecting elements arranged on a planar aperture. Each element $n$ acts as a passive scatterer whose response to an incident plane wave depends on the angle of incidence $\theta_i$, the angle of reflection $\theta_r$, the polarization, and the frequency, and is characterized by a (generally angle-dependent) reflection coefficient $\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega)$ controllable through a set of tunable parameters (e.g., bias voltages applied to varactors or PIN diodes that change the local surface impedance).

Many channel-training and channel-estimation schemes for RIS-aided wireless systems require the ability to "switch off" individual elements, meaning that the element should contribute no scattered field regardless of the directions of the incoming and outgoing waves. Formally, we say element $n$ is all-angle nulled if there exists a setting of its tunable parameters for which
$$\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega) = 0 \qquad \text{for all admissible } (\theta_i,\theta_r,\text{polarization}),$$
so that the element produces no scattered field for every incidence/reflection geometry within the operating band.

Problem. Determine whether a physically realizable RIS hardware architecture and associated control model exist that achieves all-angle nulling of an individual RIS element in the sense above. If so, describe such an architecture (specifying the unit-cell structure, the tunable mechanism, and the control rule) and prove that the resulting $\Gamma_n$ vanishes identically over all incidence and reflection angles, polarizations, and the operating frequency band. If not, characterize the fundamental electromagnetic obstructions that prevent such an all-angle null, and quantify the best achievable angular and bandwidth uniformity of the suppression $|\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega)|$ over a passive (or active) tunable unit cell.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work on RIS-aided spatial nulling (2024–2025) addresses nulling in specific directions and characterizes the existence of unimodular reflection weights producing perfect nulls in chosen directions, but acknowledges that an RIS element's response is intrinsically angle-, polarization-, and frequency-dependent. No source verifies a physically realizable design that nulls reflection from a single element across all angles simultaneously, so the question of true all-angle element deactivation appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: RIS-Aided Spatial Nulling: Algorithms, Analysis, and Nulling Limits
status_evidence.snippet: Addresses spatial nulling toward specified directions and discusses limits of perfect nulling using unimodular RIS weights.
status_evidence.claim: Nulling research focuses on chosen directions rather than achieving zero scattering across all incidence/reflection angles.

status_evidence.title: RIS-assisted near-field localization using practical phase shift model
status_evidence.snippet: An RIS affects the incident signal differently depending on the incident angle, polarization state, and reflected angle.
status_evidence.claim: RIS element response is inherently angle- and polarization-dependent, suggesting all-angle nulling is not generically achievable with standard designs.
